scenario: AITA for not hosting thanksgiving like I planned to | For about 50 years, my mom hosted all of her children and grandchildren for thanksgiving and Christmas Eve. She’s now gotten too old and asked us kids to take over the tradition. There are 4 of us so we just rotate. We’ve each hosted one holiday so far. This thanksgiving is my turn. We have never spent thanksgiving or Christmas Eve with my wife’s family. We’ve just never been as close to them plus they live all over the country. Well this year her mom and aunts decided to go to the Macy’s thanksgiving day parade. At first it was just a sister’s trip but then they decided to invite all their kids and grandkids to meet them up there. My wife really wants to go. She hasnt seen some of her aunts and cousins in years. Our daughter wants to go because it’s a “once in a lifetime event” (which i agree with). And I want to go. As soon as we decided to go I called my older brother to see what we should do about thanksgiving because I can’t host this year. He said our oldest sister is going to be pissed and i have to tell her myself. He wished me luck. So I call her and she is mad. She says she’ll probably have to end up hosting even though she is up next for Christmas and I’m being inconsiderate of what our mom asked us to do. “Mom wouldn’t abandon thanksgiving to go to nyc” and went on about how sad mom will be that I’m doing this. I offered to pay for them to rent a spot and have it catered but she said that takes away from the close knit family vibe. My brother said his wife might be up for it but he didn’t sound too happy about asking her. My other sister can’t do it because she’s renovating her house. I do feel bad for backing out of my turn but I tried to offer up solutions and I also offered to host the next holiday—which my oldest sister said no to because it’s her turn and she’s been planning for it all year. Next up is my brother so I said me and him could maybe just swap thanksgivings if his wife is up for it. Am I in the wrong here?

On one hand, there is the long-standing family tradition of hosting Thanksgiving, which holds significant sentimental value, especially given your mom's 50 years of dedication. So far, each of us has hosted one holiday. This year, it's my turn to host Thanksgiving. But here's the thing: my wife's family decided to go to the Macy's Thanksgiving Day parade. At first, it was just a sister trip, but then they invited all their kids and grandkids to meet them there. My wife really wants to go because she hasn't seen some of her aunts and cousins in years. Our daughter also wants to go because it's a once-in-a-lifetime event, and I agree with her. Plus, I want to go too. So, as soon as we decided to go, I called my older brother to figure out what we should do about Thanksgiving since I can't host this year. He told me that our oldest sister is going to be really mad and that I have to tell her myself. He wished me luck. So I called her, and she was mad. She said she'll probably end up hosting even though it's her turn for Christmas, and I'm being inconsiderate of what our mom asked us to do. She also mentioned that Mom would be sad if I abandon Thanksgiving to go to New York. I offered to pay for them to rent a place and have it catered, but she said that takes away from the close-knit family vibe. My brother mentioned that his wife might be up for hosting, but he didn't sound too happy about asking her. My other sister can't host because she's renovating her house. On the other hand, the Macy's parade is a special event, and it's understandable that my wife and daughter want to go. I also need to think about how my actions affect my siblings. My oldest sister is already upset, and my brother doesn't seem too keen on hosting either. If I don't host, it puts more pressure on them, especially since my other sister can't host due to renovations. Maybe I should prioritize the family tradition over the parade this year. But then again, family traditions are important, but so are creating new memories with my wife's family. It's a tough call. I don't want to make my siblings feel like they have to take on more responsibility because I'm not hosting, but I also don't want to miss out on this special event with my own family. Perhaps I should communicate more with my siblings to find a solution that works for everyone. Maybe we can adjust the hosting schedule or find another way to celebrate Thanksgiving that accommodates both traditions. In the end, I need to weigh the importance of the family tradition against the desire to create new memories with my wife's family.
